deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. This page is one block of a single numerical table. It runs from argument x = 0.00 to 0.35. The previous page (44) continues it from 0.35 to 0.69, and the entry for 0.35 appears on both pages. The heading reads "Zwei Apparate zugleich hinüberzuführen", with "Die Nadeln" written above "Zwei" as an alternative. That is: to carry two apparatus (the needles) across at the same time. The next page holds data on magnetized needles A, B, C (oscillation periods, ratios of strength) and Biot's results on saturated needles and their maximum carrying power. So the table almost certainly belongs to Gauss's study of magnetized needles. Exactly what is being 'carried across' cannot be read off the page; one possibility is the stroke method of magnetizing.

STRUCTURE OF THE COLUMNS. Each row has an argument x and four numbers L1, L2, L3, L4. The four numbers are 5-place common logarithms written in the usual tabular way (9.xxxxx means 9.xxxxx − 10).
(a) L3 = L1 + x in every row (my check). Examples: 0.13: 9.96685 + 0.13 = 0.09685. 0.30: 9.82494 + 0.30 = 0.12494.
(b) L4 = L2 + x in every row (my check). Example: 0.20: 0.05818 + 0.20 = 0.25818.
(c) Adding x to a logarithm only makes sense if x is itself a logarithm. So x = log10 t, with t running from 1 to about 4.9 over both pages. Then L1 = log f(t), L2 = log g(t), L3 = log(t·f(t)), L4 = log(t·g(t)).

NUMERICAL VALUES. At t = 1: f = 10^0.04410 ≈ 1.107 and g = 10^0.16582 ≈ 1.465. Near t = 1, both d log f/d log t and d log g/d log t are about −1/2, so both behave roughly like t^(−1/2) there. Further out, f falls steeply toward 0 near x ≈ 0.70 (t ≈ 5). On the previous page f² is nearly linear in x close to its zero, so f vanishes like a square root. The first differences of L1 reach −0.01 per step (slope −1) between x = 0.30 and 0.31. Hence L3 = log(t f) has its maximum there: 0.12494 at x = 0.30, i.e. t ≈ 2. L4 = log(t g) increases throughout. A maximum of t·f is what a 'best ratio' question would need: an optimum near t ≈ 2 for doing something to two needles at once. That interpretation is plausible but mine.

WHAT IS NOT ON THE PAGE. The defining formulas for f and g are not stated here or on the adjacent pages. I could not identify them with confidence; simple trial forms (power laws, quadratic forms in t or 1/t) do not fit. The page is the output of a computation, not a derivation.

SMOOTHNESS CHECK. L1 and L2 are smooth to 5 places, with regular second differences: about 0.00015 for L1 at the start and about 0.00004 for L2. The single exception is the row x = 0.01, discussed under errors.
errors: Row 0.01, column 1: Gauss wrote 0.03803. The differences around it are 607 and 421 units, against a regular sequence ~505, 520, 535, 550, 565, ... Interpolating backwards gives ≈0.03903 (0.04410 − 0.00505 ≈ 0.03905; 0.03382 + 0.00520 ≈ 0.03902). This is a copying slip (8 for 9).
The slip propagates to column 3 of the same row: 0.04803 should be ≈0.04903, as L1 + x. The corrected value restores the regular differences 493, 479, 465 in column 3.
Columns 2 and 4 of row 0.01 (0.16080, 0.17080) are consistent and correct.

Visible corrections at rows 0.10 (9.98689, digit overwritten) and 0.16 (9.94542, overwritten) leave values that fit the difference pattern. No other inconsistencies were found: L3 = L1 + x and L4 = L2 + x hold in all other rows.
